guidance.opening:
It is autumn 1920 in Boston. You sit in a landlord’s small office because he sent for someone who could look into a property that will not stay rented. Papers and a set of keys rest on the desk, unused.

“I’m Steven Knott. I inherited an old house nobody will keep. Last tenants ran after some kind of disaster—neighbors talk, and I can’t let a place sit empty forever. I want a sensible person to find out what’s wrong and get its name clear. Day work, if you take it. We haven’t shaken on anything yet.”

He folds his hands and looks you over. “So who are you, and what do you do for a living? Rough answer’s fine.”
guidance.advice: Use only listed occupation names. 1920s Boston daylight hire by a landlord; public work is looking into why a house will not stay rented and clearing its reputation—research at papers or records, neighbors, former tenants, or the house itself later, none of that decided here. Strong public fits: Private Investigator, Journalist, Lawyer, Police Detective, Police Officer, Professor, Librarian, Antiquarian, Author, Doctor of Medicine, Parapsychologist, Engineer, Dilettante. Clergy or Missionary can be public if the player wants a pastoral angle; Criminal, Drifter, Soldier, Military Officer, Athlete, Artist, Entertainer, Farmer, Musician, Pilot, Zealot, Tribe Member are playable if the player supplies a reason Knott would send for them. Skip Hacker as anachronistic. Useful training: Library Use, History, Law, Credit Rating, Persuade, Fast Talk, Spot Hidden, Listen, Psychology, Occult as rumor-interest not certainty. Languages optional: English assumed; Latin or Italian only if the player invents a personal reason. Belongings: 1920s street clothes, notebook, pencil, streetcar fare, pocket watch; no keys, cash advance, or address yet. Optional ties: Boston local vs. out-of-towner, why a landlord’s notice reached them, money vs. curiosity. Do not invent numbers, force a profession, or treat background as fact. Do not hand over commission, keys, or pay.
guidance.handoff: The visitor has only met landlord Steven Knott in his Boston office in autumn 1920. He has explained a public hire to look into an unrented inherited house and restore its name; no handshake, no daily fee, no keys, address, or cash. Identity and occupation are still being established. Continue from that meeting; do not treat the commission as accepted or items as acquired.
